### Rewilding life scripts, rebuilding institutions

Back in college, I had a funny fascination with the contemporaneous New York Life commercials. They were eloquent paeans to institutions as arbiters of progress, spanning a skyline from say a century ago to a century or so in the future. 

![](/media/n8e22pz9.png)
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ohbr0RTBvWs

That generational change definitely feels apropos for kids of my generation, particularly the ambitious, diligent sort that went to a *good* college and dutifully joining the professional managerial class. 

I was catching up with an old friend from undergrad earlier. and our conversation touched on some of those themes. He wrote a blog post that touches on the key trends:
> "long arc of institutional transformation: from the community-centered trust described by Putnam, to the meritocratic faith of Brooks’ organizational kids, to the widespread skepticism documented by Twenge." https://abhinemani.com/blog/2024/12/28/Organizational-Kid/

Part of the reason everything feels so apocalyptic is that institutions are obviously failing. It's not just that the world has problems (tm) or that those interrelate into what some call a polycrisis, much of the angst and sense of doom stems from our clear collective inability to act. 

Rather than list all the familiar challenges about why its hard to build or why our core institutions don't take the climate crisis seriously or why life scripts like joining a company that lets you buy a house and raise a family are scrambled, I'd like to take an oblique angle. 

I read somewhere that burnout comes from caring and trying to change something that you fundamentally can't control for long periods of time. Obviously big challenges like the impacts of climate change dwarf a human life. But there is a sense in which that you can't join something that lets you be part of the solution. 

Part of that is definitely personal and the evolution of an ambitious young man into middle age. There is also the sense in which the core institutions that we rely on for continuity may no longer exist in the same shape or form. I wrote about similar themes earlier looking at our democratic experiment in self government: 

> "Something does definitely very very awry. The old signposts of civic life continue on though there's a need to pass the torch. The implicit protocol for public meetings, like a recent fire safety council one, is a monthly or bimonthly in person get together plus lots of information shared on dead pieces of trees. Those tend to be well moderated and have a substrate of civility. Then there's what happens online where there can be name calling and all the stuff that you see in what passes for civic discourse at the national level these days." https://blyg.pioneeringspirit.xyz/t/6kgc4qs9cyqr1typ6grn3m3w7c/

Some of the obvious questions go towards:
1. Where are greenshoots of new institutions? 
2. How might we shorten the Gramsci gap? 
3. What historical periods are most analogous? 

I am very intrigued by new efforts like Edge Esmeralda, albeit am interested in building institutions at the center of civic life. (More the second foundation on Trantor rather than the Terminus energy of Edge.) 

I have some thoughts on tools to increase capacity to address problems. [One angle I explored is credit rating agencies as an inspiration for performance management. The idea is that an independent party applying a consistent yardstick to how reliably an organization meets its commitments might be a better model for judging whether teams and institutions are delivering than relying on their own self-reporting. It's one way to make an institution's capacity legible and credible to the people who depend on it: https://blyg.pioneeringspirit.xyz/t/3y5dn6ee43f7rymwcnbd0csb2p/] 

And I am very curious to continue exploring all those questions. Looking forward to finding more kindred spirits and inquisitive collaborators in *The Thicket*.
